issues.title: The borrowing loop mechanism for leverage makes all traders using leverage subject to liquidation
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L309


# Vulnerability details

### Impact

[docs.compound.finance/v2/ctokens/#liquidate-borrow](https://docs.compound.finance/v2/ctokens/#liquidate-borrow)

Leveraged position are compounded using a loop by using the max borrow capacity at each time. meaning that if the quote token the user is trading just drop a little in value a liquidator will be allow to liquidate his position until the user close his trade.

### Proof of Concept

The Position contract create leveraged position by borrowing multiple time the full available liquidity ([Position.sol#L309](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L309) - [Position.sol#L267](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L267))

This technique allow to high leveraged position (up to x3) but don’t let any margin in case the supplied token loss value against the quote token (which, at some point, will be the case for long and short positions). 

But when the supplied token will decrease a little in value a liquidator will be allow to seize the trader position until the trade end by calling the native Compound function `liquidateBorrow()` [CErc20.sol#L115-L118](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/compound-v2-fork/CErc20.sol#L115-L118)

### Recommended Mitigation Steps

The borrowing loop mechanism must allow room for price changes. Instead of borrowing all the available liquidity at every loop this is needed to adjust the max borrowing amount depending of the leverage choose by the trader to let the trader position organically end.

issues.title: Setting a v2 offer owner with address(0) will trick `RubiconMarket.buy()` to think it's dealing with a v1 offer and it will silently lose funds instead of reverting.
Automatic matching allows front running offers forcing the maker to pay fees instead of earning them
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L824-L852


# Vulnerability details

If maker fees are enabled and high enough and given the orderbook depth is low enough above the offer,  front running by an  opposite offer at the same price becomes profitable by forcing the maker to pay protocol fees, the maker fee to the attacker and preventing him from receiving the intended maker fee. Issue is less severe in markets with bigger spreads, but markets with higher volume tend to have lower spreads, hence it's greater for the more important markets.

## Impact
1. Loss of funds by the maker
2. If the maker is a strategists, loss of funds by the LPs 
3. Chaotic price action, 
4. in the long run, issues with liquidity caused by thin order books around the market price.

## Proof of Concept
Take a stable coin pair A, B. Let:
market price = 1 
protocolFee = 10pbs 
makerFee = 10bps
orderbookDepth = 3000 A

Maker sends a tx with offer to buy B at a price below below the orderbookDepth
pay_gem = A
pay_amt =  10000
buy_gem = B
buy _amt =  10001


Attacker front runs with an offer
pay_gem = B
pay_amt = 13001
buy_gem = A
buy _amt =  13000

Front runner fills the 3000 worth of orders paying protocol + maker fees 
attackPayed = 3000*20bps = 6
Original offer fills front runners offer for 10000, paying 
attackEarned = 10000 * 10pbs = 10 

Yielding attacker  with
attackNet = attackEarned - attackPayed = 4

Overall losses of the Maker are
makerLoss = 10000 * (makerFee + protocolFee + lostMakerFee) = 30


## Tools Used
VS Code, Pen and paper
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Allow the maker to chose if they want the offer to be matched. It can be done in many ways eg.
1. add a `bool doMatch` parameter to offer
2. never match offers from strategists, let `offer()` verify if `msg.sender` is part of some kind of strategist registry

issues.title: `RubiconMarket._buys` will not work for V1 offers due to the reversion in `cancel` method.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L1201-L1202


# Vulnerability details


## Impact
`RubiconMarket._buys` tries to cancel dust remaining offers, but it fails for V1 offers. So it blocks `RubiconMarket._buys`.


## Proof of Concept

In `RubiconMarket._buys`, it tries to cancel an offer with dust pay token amount after fulfilling. So it sets `dustId` so it can pass the `RubiconMarket.can_cancel` modifier.

```solidity
        if (
            isActive(id) &&
            offers[id].pay_amt < _dust[address(offers[id].pay_gem)]
        ) {
            dustId = id; //enable current msg.sender to call cancel(id)
            cancel(id);
        }
```

But when we move into `cancel` method, there is another validation. `RubiconMarket.cancel` will call `SimpleMarket.cancel`, and `SimpleMarket.cancel` tries to return dust pay token amount to owner.

```solidity
        _offer.owner == address(0) && msg.sender == _offer.recipient
            ? require(_offer.pay_gem.transfer(_offer.recipient, _offer.pay_amt))
            : require(_offer.pay_gem.transfer(_offer.owner, _offer.pay_amt));
```

In this case, `msg.sender` is different from `_offer.recipient` so `SimpleMarket.cancel` will treat this as a V2 offer, while it can be a valid V1 offer. So for a V1 offer, it tries to send pay token amount to `_offer.owner`, and it is `address(0)` for V1 offers. So it will revert and `SimpleMarket.cancel` will not work although it passes `RubiconMarket.can_cancel` modifier. This will block `_buy` method.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps


In `SimpleMarket.cancel`, we should refund pay token amount to `_offer.recipient` when `_offer.owner` is `address(0)`.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L1066


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`RubiconMarket.sellAllAmount` returns a meaningless, wrong value.

## Proof of Concept

`RubiconMarket.sellAllAmount` calculates `fill_amt` and then returns fee deducted value of it. 

```solidity
    fill_amt = calcAmountAfterFee(fill_amt);
```

`fill_amt` is in offer's pay token, and fee is deducted from offer's buy token. So deducting fee from `fill_amt` is meaningless and not correct. When we handle the fee, it should be added to `pay_amt` parameter of `sellAllAmount`. So `sellAllAmount` returns a meaningless value. In `Position` contract, this return value is not used, and `Position` is safe. But EOAs and other contracts also can interact with `RubiconMarket`, so this problem should be noticed.


## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

We can safely remove the last line of `RubiconMarket.sellAllAmount`.

```solidity
 -      fill_amt = calcAmountAfterFee(fill_amt);
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L8


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The FeeWrapper contract can be used to wrap calls to arbitrary contracts to include a fee for a third party. The contract at a high level works as follows:

1. User calculates fee for amount
2. User calls FeeWrapper with the proper params and amounts (total and fee)
3. FeeWrapper takes funds from user
4. FeeWrapper sends fee amount to fee recipient
5. FeeWrapper calls the target contract, forwarding the amount. In the case of an ERC20 it approves the spend, in case of ETH it sends the value as call value.

The general approach sounds ok, however there is an important detail that will conflict with most contract implementations. In point 5 the caller to the target is the FeeWrapper itself, not the original user. This means that in the context of the target contract, `msg.sender` is the FeeWrapper contract. For example, a swap action in a decentralized exchange will return the swapped assets back to the caller. A deposit on a lending protocol will associate the collateral with the caller of the function, and only the caller will be able to eventually redeem that collateral.

The potential impact of the issue will depend on the case, but it certainly can be high for many cases. We will explore a few situations of loss of funds for the `RubiconRouter` contract in the next section.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/periphery/BathBuddy.sol#L38


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The `BathBuddy` contracts implements rewards for liquidity providers (holders of `BathToken`). The contract is modeled after the famous Synthetix staking contract, with some tweaks to support rewards for multiple tokens at the same time.

The implementation overall is correct, however there is a critical difference with the Synthetix contract that is ignored in the `BathBuddy` contract. In the Synthetix implementation the main actions related to rewards accounting are the `stake` and `withdraw` actions, these trigger the `updateReward` modifier to ensure correct reward accounting. Staked tokens cannot be transferred, as these are held in the staking contract. In the BathBuddy implementation things are very different as there is no staking, rewards are intended to be distributed directly to holders of the BathToken without any need of staking the tokens in the contract. This means that, as there is no "staking" action in the BathBuddy implementation (i.e. depositing funds in the contract), rewards fail to be correctly accounted whenever BathToken are minted, burned or transferred between different accounts.

These are two critical places in the code where the BathBuddy contract uses the state from the BathToken, but fails to be triggered whenever the state in the BathToken is modified. # Vulnerability details


## Impact
The BathBuddy contract assumes that all ERC20 tokens (referred to as "myBathTokenBuddy" in the contract) are always staked. The staking reward should be distributed based on the time-weighted share of each user of the total myBathTokenBuddy supply (see: [math explainer](https://twitter.com/ProgrammerSmart/status/1545637246543736833?t=dzVIFWPvIZJnOUqxSUSoVw&s=33), [video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LWWsjw3cgDk). 

However, this is not the case:
The BathBuddy contract does not update the reward for the user before the transfer is executed. Instead, the BathBuddy contract updates the reward for the user only when the user calls the `updateReward` function. This means that the user can transfer the tokens to another address, and the reward will be lost. Additionally, an attacker can call the `updateReward` function once, move their tokens to another address, and call the `updateReward` function again. This will result in the attacker receiving the reward multiple times. A skilled attacker could potentially take the vast majority of the reward pool by using a flashloan.

1)The user calls the updateReward function in the contract.
2)The user transfers the funds to another address.

Canceling V1 offer in closed V2 market will refund to address(0)
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L459-L461


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When market is closed, anyone can call `cancel(id)` to cancel an offer. For offers made on market V1 and closed in market V2, this will result in the transfer of the `pay_gem` to `address(0)` resulting in a loss of fund for the owner of the offer.

## Proof of Concept
After migration of V1 to V2, offers made in a V1 market will have `offer.recipient = old_owner` and `offer.owner = address(0)`.

The code to decide whom to send the funds to is the following:

```solidity
    _offer.owner == address(0) && msg.sender == _offer.recipient
        ? require(_offer.pay_gem.transfer(_offer.recipient, _offer.pay_amt))
        : require(_offer.pay_gem.transfer(_offer.owner, _offer.pay_amt));
```

If V1 offer is canceled by an address that is not the V1 offer recipient then `msg.sender != _offer.recipient` and the `pay_gem` will be transferred to `_offer.owner` which is `address(0)`.

The modifier `can_cancel(id)` is the following:

```solidity
modifier can_cancel(uint256 id) virtual override {
    require(isActive(id));
    require(

As confirmed with the contest sponsor, the `FeeWrapper` contract should be able to execute calls on the `RubiconRouter` as demonstrated in `2023-04-rubicon/contracts/periphery/Test3rdPartyProtocol.sol`. # Vulnerability details

The `RubiconMarket` functions `batchOffer` and `batchRequote` both contain calls to `offer` as follows.
```Solidity
this.offer(
    payAmts[i],
    ERC20(payGems[i]),
    buyAmts[i],
    ERC20(buyGems[i])
);
```
But calling `offer` using `this.offer` will [use a message call instead of a jump](https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/v0.8.19/control-structures.html#function-calls).
This means that in `offer`, the value of `msg.sender` will be the address of the `RubiconMarket` contract, not of the original sender. Hence the offer will be made by the `RubiconMarket` itself.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

An account holding bathTokens can get rewards payed out by the BathBuddy independently of how long the tokens had been held. In particular, an attacker can acquire some bathTokens, collect the rewards, transfer the bathTokens to a fresh account, collect the rewards again, and repeat this until all reward tokens held by the BathBuddy contract have been drained.

Via the `BathHouseV2` function `claimRewards`, any account can cause the `BathBuddy`'s `getReward` function to be called (with the account address as the second argument). issues.title: Opening leveraged long / short positions can be frontrun
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L460-L472


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A user may get sandwiched when opening a position. This results in worse prices for him and worsens the experience on the Rubicon platform.   

## Proof of Concept
We calculate both the `buy_amt` and the `max_fill_amount` for on-chain. This allows attackers to sandwich these traders. 

```solidity
buyAllAmount(ERC20 buy_gem, uint256 buy_amt, ERC20 pay_gem, uint256 max_fill_amount)
```


```solidity
uint256 _buyAmount = rubiconMarket.getBuyAmount(
    ERC20(_asset),
    ERC20(_quote),
    _maxFill.sub(_fee)
);

rubiconMarket.buyAllAmount(
    ERC20(_asset),
    _buyAmount,
    ERC20(_quote),
    _maxFill
);
```
Since neither the amount entered nor the amount returned is checked for soundness, an attacker can arbitrarily change the market conditions before the trade to degrade the users` expected leverage.
This results in users paying much more than they expected to receive the desired amount of `_minFill` tokens. This may result in them having much higher leverage than expected and being liquidated.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

We should either 1) calculate one of the two parameters off-chain and then pass it to the function, or 2) compare the values with an oracle price and revert if the two values differ too much.
1) has some implementation problems, since a user would have to calculate all the minimum amounts along the path. A more technical sound solution it to predict an acceptable *realized* leverage value.
2) is a technically simpler solution, but would only put an upper limit on the MEV that can be extracted from the user.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L282

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L87


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

When a user calls `closePosition(..)` -> `_repay(..)` on the `Position` contract, the function `borrowBalanceOfPos(..)` is used to calculate the amount that the user needs to repay. This repayment amount is equivalent to the amount the user borrowed (`_borrowedAmount`) plus their interest (`_interest`). To calculate this interest portion, the function multiplies the current borrowRate by the difference in number of blocks between when the user created the position and the current block timestamp. The issue arises because the borrowRate over the entire duration of the borrow is defined as: `rate = CTokenInterface(bathToken).borrowRatePerBlock();`. However `borrowRatePerBlock()` is a function of total borrows and total supply for the cToken, thus is not required to be the same over the entire duration of when the user takes out their position. This means the calculated repayment amount can potentially overshoot or undershoot the actual amount.

## Proof of Concept

Steps:
    1. Bob uses the Position contract to open a leveraged position using the `buyAllAmountWithLeverage(..)` function, this results in an increased borrow interest rate
    2. Later, Alice also uses the Position contract to open a leveraged position using the `buyAllAmountWithLeverage(..)` function, this again results in an increased borrow interest rate
    3. Bob calls `closePosition(..)`, where the call to `_repay(..)` references the current `borrowRatePerBlock()` which prices Bob's interest at the rate which includes Bob

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Currently there is no slippage check in function `_rubiconSwap()`. This function will trade whatever amount and price. But when the liquidity is low, users could lose fund due to high slippage. Malicious users could even frontrun the swap call in open position or repay function to take advantage of other users, similar to "sandwich" attack.


## Proof of Concept


Function `_rubiconSwap()` -> `_marketBuy()/_marketSell()` -> `RubiconMarket.sol#getBuyAmount()/getPayAmount()` -> `RubiconMarket.sol#buyAllAmount()/sellAllAmount()` will be called for the swap. With no slippage check for all the trades, in `RubiconMarket.sol`, `getBuyAmount()/getPayAmount()` and `buyAllAmount()/sellAllAmount()` just add all the offers with any given price. But when the depth is shadow, some offers could have abnormal price. Users have to pay much more than normal price. So users could lose some fund due to high slippage.

443:     function _rubiconSwap(
444:         address _asset,
445:         address _quote,

448:     ) internal {

450:             ? _marketBuy(_asset, _quote, _fillLimit)

```

is invalid since there needs to be a check for the number of decimals for the underlying asset/bath token.

Miscalculation of the maximum amount that can be borrowed.

Consider checking for each underlying bath token decimal
e.g.

## Impact

The SpawnBuddy contract is designed to handle the vesting of ERC20 tokens for a given Bath Token. However, there is an access control issue within the contract that could potentially lead to unauthorized access to funds and manipulation of the contract state.

Details:

The access control issue is present in the spawnBuddy function. The function is marked as external and has no access control modifiers, allowing anyone to call it. When the spawnBuddy function is called for the first time, the friendshipStarted variable is set to true at the end of the function execution.

This line does limit the attack vector to some extent by preventing multiple calls to the spawnBuddy function after the initial setup. However, it does not fully mitigate the risk associated with the lack of access control in the function. An attacker can still call the spawnBuddy function before the legitimate owner does, modifying the owner, myBathTokenBuddy, and bathHouse addresses, and setting the friendshipStarted flag to true. This would effectively lock out the legitimate owner from setting up the contract correctly and give the attacker control over the contract.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/1cd6d4e84c510c70c9062e2d6f961502f50aa097/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L105


# Vulnerability details



## Impact

In case of incorrect input calculation, the 3rd party send more token than needed.
And, Rubicon does not spend all `approval` token due to wrong input `arg`.

This can cause stuck token in `FeeWrapper.sol` contract.

Any abuser can drain any leftover token in `FeeWrapper.sol` contract.

## Proof of Concept

- User make a call to `FeeWrapper.sol` with `totalAmount` of token
- Fee was taken and approve `Rubicon` contract to spend `totalAmount - fee` [token based on user input](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/1cd6d4e84c510c70c9062e2d6f961502f50aa097/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L105)
- But the `seletor` and `args` params are incorrect.
- The rubicon contract does not spend all approval token.
- There will be left over token in `FeeWrapper.sol` contract that have no `sweepToken` method.
- Since approval amount still have some left over, next abuser can simply make a rubicall with no fee. And let `Rubicon` contracts spend the leftover token.

## Tools Used

Manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Either add free `sweepTokens()` method for everyone with warning comment. And let 3rd party handle faulty input.

Or implement no-balance-change check after external call. Do not use zero-balance check as anyone can send token and brick the contract.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `rubicall()` function lacks any input validation for the parameters passed to it:

```
    struct CallParams {
        bytes4 selector; // function selector
        bytes args; // encoded arguments (abi.encode() || abi.encodePacked)
        address target; // target contract to call
        FeeParams feeParams;
    }

    struct FeeParams {
        address feeToken; // token in the form of which fee paid
        uint256 totalAmount; // amount without deducted fee
        uint256 feeAmount; // amount of feeToken from which fee should be charged

    }
```
This open the gates to many possibilities for misuse of the functions used in FeeWrapper.sol. Please, find more information in the PoC section.

**No validation for totalAmount and feeAmount**

Any address and function selector can be passed and subsequently executed. This poses a risk for the users, so a malicious contract can be passed calling a function to whatever the attacker likes. E.g unauthorized approval of an ERC20 token spend etc.

Manual Review

Anytime a user deposit to BathToken update the userRewardsPerTokenPaid[token][account] immediately, then when he try to get rewards rewardPerToken(token).sub(userRewardsPerTokenPaid[token][account]) will be zero and exploitation can be avoided.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
When a third party protocol wants to engage the Rubicon Market, low level calls can revert, causing 
a loss of funds and ETH being stuck in the contract.

## Proof of Concept
Assume that the "require" statement in the ```_chargeFeePayable``` function fails due to an incorrect "msg.value" 
being sent, which means that the "msg.value" is not equal to "_totalAmount" as expected. This could be in excess
of the expected amount for example.

The ```require(OK, "ETH transfer failed");``` statement will then also fail, resulting in another revert. 

Since the function is not handling the revert with a refund mechanism or reverting the entire transaction,

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A normal user can't cancel his offer when using a specific API.

## Proof of Concept

1. The function [`offer`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L511) of `SimpleMarket` is not overridden by the `RubiconMarket` contract.
(Note that this function is called in the testing [example](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/test/foundry-tests/ProtocolDeployment.t.sol#L89))

2. The [`cancel`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L452) function inside `SimpleMarket` is overridden by the [`cancel`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L871) function in `RubiconMarket`.

## Impact
The `BathBuddy` contract allows liquidity providers (`bathToken` holders) to earn additional ERC-20 token rewards. 
In this contract, `admin` can set the reward duration and during this duration `liquidity providers` earn reward tokens. 
The amount of reward tokens depends on the amount of `bathtoken` they have and the total supply of `bathtoken`. 
Generally, the amount of reward tokens that liquidity providers receive is calculated as `(total reward amount) * (bathtoken amount of liquidity provider) / (total supply of bathtoken)`. 
At the end of the duration, all rewards are consumed. 
However, when a user opens a position (long or short), it repeats `supply collateral → borrow → swap`, so that his position contract holds some `bathTokens`.
When the position contract supplies collateral, it receives `bathTokens` instead of the underlying tokens. 
Since this contract has some of the `bathToken`, the total supply of `bathToken` increases, 
Then, reward tokens cannot be withdrawn for the number of `bathTokens` held by the position contract.
It means the reward tokens are locked

`rewardsDuration` = 365*24*60*60
`total reward amount` = 10000 Reward Tokens
`total supply of bathToken` = 1000
`Amount of bathToken that are minted by opening position` = 500
As a result, 5000 Reward Tokens will be locked

Vs code

The loss amount will be the sum of all deposits done by users into the CToken multiplied by the underlying token's price.

This attack has been documented previously , for reference : [https://www.akshaysrivastav.com/articles/first-deposit-bug-in-compound-v2](https://www.akshaysrivastav.com/articles/first-deposit-bug-in-compound-v2)

The formulas used in the CToken contracts can be reduced to the following:

```solidity
Exchange rate = underlying.balanceOf(CToken) * 1e18 / CToken.totalSupply()

CToken amount = User deposit amount / Exchange rate
```

If the exchange rate can be increased greater than a user’s deposit the CToken amount would be 0 because of the division.

Once the bathtoken is deployed the attacker can mint the smallest possible amount of the token and transfer underlying token to the contract, thus artificially inflating the `underlying.balanceOf(CToken)` value. 

Then for the next user will get 0 CTokens against their deposit.

For more details kindly refer the above mentioned article.

### Recommendation Mitigation Steps

In the BathHouseV2 contract, a small amount of underlying tokens can be deposited as the initial deposit and then burn the received CTokens by sending them to a dead address.

# Vulnerability details

## Summary

There is no slippage control in `buyAllAmount` and `sellAllAmount` within the Rubicon orderbook. This will open up room for a front-running attack that extracts value from user's market trades, also causing them to receive less than expected.

## Proof of concept

This attack behaves similar to the sandwich attack, commonly seen in MEV bots on AMM tradings.

0. Assuming the orderbook has the following limit offers (this is taken from the actual Rubicon V1 orderbook at the time of writing)
    - 0.04 ETH for 72 USDC (price: 1800)
    - 0.12 ETH for 210 USDC (price: 1750)
    - 0.21 ETH for 364 USDC (price: 1733)
    - 0.48 ETH for 816 USDC (price: 1700)
1. Alice wants to sell 0.37 ETH. According to the current orderbook, she should fill the first three orders, for a total of 646 USDC.
2. Alice sends the transaction. Bob notices this and front-runs with a transaction as follow:
    - Bob market-sells 0.37 ETH for a total of 646 USDC.
    - Bob places a limit order, selling 0.37 ETH for 629.37 USDC (price: 1701 USDC).
3. Alice transaction goes through before Bob's. She only receives 629.37 USDC. 

Bob has immediately arbitraged 16.63 USDC from Alice's trade. Alice's market order receives less than expected.

## Impact

Loss of funds for users making market orders.

## Tools used

Manual review + inspecting protocol V1

## Recommended mitigation steps

Add a slippage control mechanism to market orders. This must be added to `Positions` as well, to prevent margin positions being sniped similarly, as they also utilize market orders.

# Vulnerability details


## Impact

The `FeeWrapper` contract poses significant risks, as its usage together with certain Router functions can lead to a **loss of funds**.

Several functions within the `Router` send funds back to the `msg.sender`, which in this case is the `FeeWrapper` contract, rather than the user. 

This occurs because not all functions in the Router utilize a dedicated `to` address variable for returning funds.

As a result, ERC20 tokens can become trapped within the `FeeWrapper` contract and subsequently be stolen by any malicious actor.

## Proof of Concept

The `feeWrapper` is called by a `ThirdPartyProtocol` to perform a call to a router function.

The contract call chain will be:
```
User -> 3rdPartyProtocol -> FeeWrapper -> Router -> RubiconMarket
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L505-L510


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The contract Position.sol does buys and sells of leveraged amounts. However it has no inbuilt slippage protection, making them vulnerable to sandwich attacks.

Due to the nature of the rubicon market contract, it has no in-built slippage protections, which revert when certain limits are hit. This can be an issue since MEV is a constant threat, removing sell orders before a user's buy order in order to give them a worse price.

The Position contract, is also vulnerable to the same issue, but leveraged up. This makes it a juicy target for MEV bots since there are multiple buys and sells within a single transaction. If an MEV bot removes a large amount of sell and buy orders ion the market by filling them, it forces the position contract to operate leveraged trades with a bad spread. The MEV bot can then backrun the user's call to fill in the spread and profit off of the difference.

## Proof of Concept
Consider an MEV bot sandwiches a 200ETH transaction, with 2x leverage. USDC provided as collateral, and ETH is longed.
1. MEV bot removes ETH sell orders by buying them up, giving the user's transaction a bad ETH buy price.
2. User's transaction is included. ETH is bought at a bad price and looped multiple times to achieve leverage required.
3. MEV bot puts up sell orders on the eth bought in step 1. This eth is sold off due to arbitragers, since the price has been pulled down artificially.

MEV happens in every block, and the only real protection against them is slippage, since even services like flashbots are now susceptible to bad actors. Thus a lack of slippage protection makes this a high severity issue.

## Tools Used
Manual Review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add slippage protection in Rubicon Market, and in Position.sol

## Impact

Link to how the oracle gets underlying price - https://docs.compound.finance/v2/prices/#underlying-price

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

**Due to trust in the Rubicon team, the external contract approves the maximum value to FeeWrapper before calling `rubicalls`, and not revoke approval after the interaction**. Then, the attacker can call `rubicalls` with carefully constructed parameters that encode `erc20.transferFrom(external, attack, amount)`, resulting in the external contract's token being stolen.

Before the external contract interacts with the Rubicon contract by `rubicalls`, the token must be approved to FeeWrapper. The external contract **approves the maximum value of a certain token** to FeeWrapper, and **the approval of this token is not revoked** after the interaction. Then the attacker can steal the token of the external contract through the following code:

```solidity
/*
        token:  valuable token
        victim: external contract
        to:     attacker's address
        amount: token amount

    function fun(address token, address victim, address to, uint256 amount) {

        FeeWrapper.CallParams memory params = FeeWrapper.CallParams(
            ERC20.transferFrom.selector,
            abi.encode(victim, to, route, amount),
            token,
            feeParams
        );
        FeeWrapper(feeWrapper).rubicall(params);

```

# Lines of code

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `RubiconMarketV1`, it ensures that `info.owner = msg.sender`. But in V2 protocol, `RubiconMarket` doesn’t ensure such things. Both `recipient` and `owner` can be address(0). If a user forgets to set those parameters. the user’s payment would be stuck in the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

In `RubiconMarketV1`, it ensures that `info.owner = msg.sender`.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/periphery/RubiconMarketV1.sol#L453
```
    function offer(
        uint256 pay_amt,
        ERC20 pay_gem,
        uint256 buy_amt,
        ERC20 buy_gem
    ) public virtual can_offer synchronized returns (uint256 id) {
        …
        info.owner = msg.sender;
        …
    }
```

But in V2 protocol, it doesn’t ensure such things.  Both `recipient` and `owner` can be address(0).
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L532-L533
```
    function offer(
        uint256 pay_amt,
        ERC20 pay_gem,
        uint256 buy_amt,
        ERC20 buy_gem,
        address owner,
        address recipient
    ) public virtual can_offer synchronized returns (uint256 id) {
        …
        info.recipient = recipient;
        info.owner = owner;
        …
    }
```

If both parameters are address(0). the user cannot cancel the offer. And the user cannot receive the buy_gem from buyers.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

Add a check to make sure that at least one of `recipient` and `owner` is `msg.sender`.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Attacker can abuse the arbitrary call of `FeeWrapper.sol` contract to other contract to call transferFrom and steal other users funds/tokens

## Proof of Concept
The `FeeWrapper.sol` contract have the `rubicall` function for users to charge their own fees, this function takes a `CallParams` struct with target (address to call), selector (function to execute) and args (function's args) on behalf the `FeeWrapper` contract, 
the contract also have the `_chargeFee` function of the fee charging (free transfer), as it uses the well known allowance and transferFrom mechanism `IERC20(_feeToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _totalAmount);`, now with all of this the following scenario can occurs :

1. Alice wants to charge fee for TokenX with worth of 50 TokenX, she have 3050 TokenX
2. she calls `rubicall` which calls `_rubicall` that calls `_chargeFee`
3. `_chargeFee` will `transferFrom` Alice to `FeeWrapper.sol` on the TokenX, which ensure that Alice must have approved `FeeWrapper.sol` to spend on her behalf on TokenX (she set allowance to type(uint256).max)
4. her call succeed, now she is allowing `FeeWrapper.sol` to spend `type(uint256).max` on TokenX, and she already have 3000 worth of TokenX
5. Bob (attacker) now calls the rubicall with TokenX (repeat the steps from 2 to 4 for bob) and set the `CallParams` as :

 target = TokenX contract // target contract to call the transferFrom
 feeParams = add any
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/periphery/BathBuddy.sol#L121-L135


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
BathBuddy.rewardsPerTokensStored is not up to date as it updates only when someone claims rewards. Because of that users receive not correct rewards payment.

## Proof of Concept
`BathBuddy` is responsible for providing rewards of some token per bathToken.
Amount that should be paid for 1 bath token is calculated inside `rewardPerToken` function.
https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/periphery/BathBuddy.sol#L121-L135
```solidity
    function rewardPerToken(address token) public view returns (uint256) {
        require(friendshipStarted, "I have not started a bathToken friendship");


        if (IERC20(myBathTokenBuddy).totalSupply() == 0) {
            return rewardsPerTokensStored[token];
        }
        return
            rewardsPerTokensStored[token].add(
                lastTimeRewardApplicable(token)
                    .sub(lastUpdateTime[token])
                    .mul(rewardRates[token])
                    .mul(1e18)
                    .div(IERC20(myBathTokenBuddy).totalSupply())
            );
    }
```

You can see that `IERC20(myBathTokenBuddy).totalSupply()` is used as divisor here. This is correct as rewards should be equal to each bathToken.

The problem is that `rewardPerToken` function is only called when someone wants to [claim his rewards](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/periphery/BathBuddy.sol#L248).

But it should work in another way. `rewardsPerTokensStored` variable should calculate new amount every time bathToken is minted/burned as totalSupply is changing in that cases and `rewardsPerTokensStored` variable should too. Because of such wrong approach some users can be left without any rewards.
## Tools Used
VsCode
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
You need to update `rewardsPerTokensStored` any time bathToken is minted/burned.

# Lines of code

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/periphery/BathBuddy.sol#L168


# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability
BathToken holder(s) can abuse the `getReward()` function to claim the same BathBuddy reward, multiple times via `claim_rewards -> transfer_BathTokens_to_new_user -> claim_rewards` loop .

```
 function getReward(
        IERC20 rewardsToken,
        address holderRecipient
    )
        external
        override
        nonReentrant
        whenNotPaused
        updateReward(holderRecipient, address(rewardsToken))
        onlyBathHouse
    {
        uint256 reward = tokenRewards[address(rewardsToken)][holderRecipient];
        if (reward > 0) {
            tokenRewards[address(rewardsToken)][holderRecipient] = 0;
            rewardsToken.safeTransfer(holderRecipient, reward);
            emit RewardPaid(holderRecipient, reward);
        }
    }

```

## Impact
This allows BathToken holder(s) to drain all the rewardTokens in the BathBuddy Smart Contracts.


## Proof of Concept
 [1] `Alice` mints BathToken(s)
 [2] Holder `Alice` calls getReward() on `BathHouse` to claim BathBuddy rewards
 [3] `Alice` transfers her BathToken(s) to `Bob`
 [4] Holder `Bob` calls getReward() on `BathHouse` to claim BathBuddy rewards
 [5] `Bob` transfers the BathToken(s) to `Tim`
 [6] Rinse and repeat


## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The getReward() implementation on BathBuddy Smart Contract would need to be reviewed and ammended.

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Unprotected call to a function sending Ether to an arbitrary address.

Bob calls setDestination and withdraw. As a result he withdraws the contract's balance.

## Proof of Concept

Exploit Scenario:

```solidity
import "./FeeWrapper.sol";
contract ArbitrarySendEth{
    FeeWrapper public feewrapper;
    function setDestination(FeeWrapper msg.sender){
        feewrapper = FeeWrapper(msg.sender);
    }

    function withdraw() public{
        feewrapper.transfer(this.balance);
    }
}
```

Bob calls setDestination and withdraw. As a result he withdraws the contract's balance.

Direct links to all referenced code in GitHub:

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L76-L89

```solidity
FeeWrapper._rubicallPayable(FeeWrapper.CallParams) (contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#76-89) sends eth to arbitrary user 

	Dangerous calls: 

	- (_OK,_data) = _params.target.call{value: _msgValue}(bytes.concat(_params.selector,_params.args)) (contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#82-84) 
```

https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#L108-L121

```solidity
FeeWrapper._chargeFeePayable(FeeWrapper.FeeParams) (contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#108-121) sends eth to arbitrary user 

	Dangerous calls: 

	- (OK) = address(_feeTo).call{value: _feeAmount}() (contracts/utilities/FeeWrapper.sol#118) 
```

manual review and foundry

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Ensure that an arbitrary user cannot withdraw unauthorized funds.
